title: H2 only partly holds: outside markdowns, prices fall about 1 point of list in every category because low-discount customers stopped buying, not because accounts were repriced or new accounts got bigger discounts (~$1.43M in 2025)
conclusion: Price-to-list fell outside equipment markdowns too: parts 0.8467→0.8379, refrigeration 0.8464→0.8379, supplies 0.8465→0.8373, non-markdown equipment 0.8406→0.8281 (2016→2025, q398). Most of the equipment drop, 0.839→0.764, is H1 markdowns. The non-markdown decline is not discount creep in the sense the hypothesis meant. Customers active in both 2016 and 2025 (1,346) paid the same share of list in both years (0.8319 vs 0.8323, median change +0.0005; q413). Customers onboarded later do not carry higher discounts: cohort averages run 0.1355-0.1458 against 0.1412 for pre-2016 accounts (q404). The rise in line-weighted discount (0.1415→0.1518, q403) is a change in customer mix. Fewer low-discount accounts are still buying: of the accounts active in 2016, 0.292 of those under 10% discount were still active in 2025, against 0.4802 of those at 20% or more (q415). In 2025 that mix shift cost $1,428,556.45 on $140,533,485.01 of non-markdown list value. The within-customer rate effect was -$29,882.82, effectively zero (q418). The action is retention of standard-price accounts, not a review of discount grants. The rest of the margin decline described in H2 belongs to H1 equipment markdowns.

claims.text: Price-to-list (shipped qty, list-weighted) falls 2016→2025 in categories with no markdown lines: parts 0.8467→0.8379 (95,253 / 94,535 lines), refrigeration 0.8464→0.8379 (35,042 / 35,001), supplies 0.8465→0.8373 (75,182 / 74,356). Non-markdown equipment falls 0.8406→0.8281, while total equipment falls 0.839→0.764 as markdown lines rise from 3,744 to 18,962 of 41,020 / 49,904.

Prices follow list × (1 − customer discount) × (1 − markdown) with a stable residual. The median ratio is 0.99132 in 2016 and 0.99154 in 2025 across 280,204 and 271,831 lines. The line-weighted customer discount rises every year from 0.1415 to 0.1518.

No repricing is visible. Among 1,346 customers with non-markdown purchases in both 2016 and 2025, average price-to-list is 0.8319 vs 0.8323, median change +0.0005. Only 9 fell by more than 2 points and 13 rose by more than 2 points.
New accounts are not priced more generously. Average discount_pct by onboarding cohort ranges 0.1355-0.1458 (271-320 customers per cohort, 2016-2025), against 0.1412 for 3,154 pre-2016 customers.

The rise comes from mix within both groups. Line-weighted discount among pre-2016 customers goes from 0.1414 (271,979 lines) to 0.1565 (131,573 lines). Among customers onboarded since 2016 it goes from 0.1377 in 2018 to 0.1473 in 2025.

Low-discount accounts lapse faster. Of the customers active in 2016, the share still ordering in 2025 is 292/1,000 (0.292) for discount under 10%, 337/849 (0.3969) for 10-15%, 368/782 (0.4706) for 15-20% and 352/733 (0.4802) for 20% or more. Lines per active pre-2016 customer were similar across tiers in 2016 (83.2-93.8). The tiers have similar average credit limits and terms.

Sizing for 2025 non-markdown lines ($140,533,485.01 of list): the shortfall against 2016 price-to-list (0.8442 vs 0.8343) is $1,398,673.63. The customer-discount mix (list-weighted keep 0.8583→0.8479) accounts for $1,428,556.45, and the residual price rate for -$29,882.82.
The mix shift is broad. Line-weighted discount rose 2016→2025 in 11 of 12 branches, e.g. Fort Wayne 0.1358→0.1565, Indianapolis 0.1366→0.1575 and Troy 0.1128→0.1334. Toledo was flat (0.142→0.1402).

not_evidence_of: This is not evidence that reps or managers have been granting larger discounts, or that new accounts were signed at worse terms. Same-customer prices are flat and new cohorts are not more discounted. Nor does it show that low-discount customers left because of price: they lapse more often, but the records say nothing about why. Margin here is measured against today's static cost, so this is price erosion, not true margin.
could_not_tell: discount_pct is a single current snapshot. If the ERP re-applies the current discount to history, or lapsed customers' discounts were never updated, repricing could be hidden; discount history would be needed to rule it out. Why low-discount accounts stopped ordering (competitor, closure, consolidation) can't be told: there are no churn dates or reasons. No customer-level profitability either, so whether keeping a low-discount account is worth the effort is unknown.
next_step: List the lapsed low-discount (<10%) accounts that were active in 2016-2019 with their last order day and branch, and have account managers (by rep_id) check whether they closed or moved to a competitor. Ask IT whether discount_pct changes are logged anywhere so repricing can be ruled out directly. Split the remaining equipment price-to-list decline under H1.
dead_ends: New accounts onboarded at higher discount_pct: cohort averages 0.1355-0.1458 vs 0.1412 pre-2016 (q404)
Repricing of existing accounts: same-customer non-markdown price-to-list 0.8319→0.8323 for 1,346 customers (q413)
A residual drift in the pricing formula: median price/(list×(1−disc)×(1−md)) 0.99132 in 2016 and 0.99154 in 2025 (q403); residual rate effect -$29,882.82 (q418)
The exact formula matches only 546,426 of 2,719,712 lines to the cent (q402), so there is per-line price noise; it is stable over time and not a trend
